title: A Grand Design of Imperfections
caption: The grand design spiral galaxy NGC 5364, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 5364 · constellation Virgo · about 50 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: R. Colombari and M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Swirling arms and a glowing core mark NGC 5364 as a spiral galaxy in the constellation Virgo. Below it, a fuzzy smear is the smaller lenticular galaxy NGC 5363.

NGC 5364 is classed as a grand design spiral, a type with prominent, well-defined arms winding outward from a distinct core. Only ten percent of spirals earn the label, and because of their seemingly perfect structure they are seen as the model of what a spiral galaxy should look like.

Look closer, though, and this one has flaws. Compared with other grand design spirals, its arms are shapeless in places and lopsided. Astronomers think NGC 5363 is responsible: although it is much smaller, it sits close enough that the two pull on each other, shifting stars and gas within NGC 5364's arms and warping the galaxy's overall shape.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (22.08 x 20.70 arcminutes) and distance (50 million light years), the frame spans roughly 321,000 × 301,000 light-years. Its light set out about 50 million years before reaching the telescope.
